claims.text: Adding h-BN to a refractory high-entropy alloy matrix will reduce friction at high temperatures while retaining mechanical strength.
A refractory high-entropy alloy matrix can exhibit high mechanical strength.
The proposed refractory high-entropy alloy or ceramic matrix lacks intrinsic self-lubrication.
h-BN is a thermally robust, high-temperature-stable solid lubricant.
Approximately 10 vol% h-BN is a suitable controlled addition to the matrix.
Powder metallurgy or related composite-fabrication techniques can integrate h-BN particles into the matrix.
The composite should be evaluated from room temperature to approximately 800 °C.
Even dispersion of h-BN particles within the matrix enables formation of a lubricious interfacial film during elevated-temperature sliding.
At high temperatures, h-BN particles form a stable lubricious tribofilm at the sliding interface.
The h-BN-derived tribofilm lowers the coefficient of friction.
The refractory high-entropy alloy matrix provides load-bearing capability at elevated temperature.
Adding h-BN will not significantly impair the matrix's load-bearing capability.
Relative to pure RHEA, the h-BN composite will have lower high-temperature friction coefficient and wear rate.
The h-BN composite will maintain mechanical strength within acceptable limits for high-temperature applications.
An RHEA without solid lubricant typically has higher friction and wear at elevated temperatures despite its high strength.
Lubrication effectiveness depends on h-BN volume fraction, particle-dispersion quality, and operating temperature.
The optimal h-BN content and processing route remain undetermined and require experimental calibration.
The balance between lubrication efficiency and possible reductions in mechanical strength requires experimental optimization.
A statistically significant reduction of at least 20% in high-temperature friction and wear is the specified success threshold.
